Combination HRP2-PLDH Kantor et al., 2021, developed the Antibody-free Dual-biomarker Rapid Enrichment Workflow (AnDREW) to purify PLDH and HRP2 from large blood samples (150 μL). The analytical sensitivity for HRP2 and PLDH detection was improved by 11 and 9 times, respectively, using the AnDREW-enhanced RDTs in comparison to the unenhanced RDTs. Additionally, the limit of detection for PLDH was improved by 11 times (3.80 parasites/μL) using the AnDREW-enhanced RDTs in comparison to the unenhanced RDTs (42.31 parasites/μL). The sensitivity obtained by PLDH and HRP2 increased before and after the unenhanced method, where the PLDH sensitivity ranged from 0.7456 to 6.605 based on the slope of the best-fit line, corresponding to a 9-fold increase. The sensitivity of HRP2 ranged from 1.162 to 13.25 based on the slope of the best-fit line, corresponding to an 11-fold increase. The advantages of this method are the use of cheaper eluents and that the eluted PLDH is not complexed with molecular recognition elements [ ]. 7.4. Combination HRP2-Aldolase In the study by Akotet et al., 2013, malaria detection was carried out using the PfHRP2/pan aldolase combination rapid diagnostic test method. Using microscopy as the gold standard, 592 feverish individuals in Gabon, Central Africa, had malaria species diagnosed. The detection sensitivity was at or above 96.0% for Plasmodium falciparum and 62.5% for non- P. falciparum malaria species, with higher sensitivity in younger children (100%). The detection method used had a specificity of 87.3% and a false positive rate of 27.1%. Overall, 32.5% of all tests produced “faint bands”, and only two resulted from samples with parasitemia below 100 p/μL. The advantage of this method is it only detects live parasites. Furthermore, the aldolase gene is highly conserved. However, it is limited by the low prevalence of non- P. falciparum malaria infections [ ]. 7.5. Hemozoin Yadav et al., 2022, describe the use of magnetic surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (M-SERS) to detect hemozoin, a metabolic byproduct of the malaria parasite that exhibits paramagnetic characteristics. Its advantage compared to measurements conducted on the traditional SERS substrates without any magnetic field is that the SERS signal intensity was increased tenfold. For M-SERS, the hemozoin detection limit was as low as 10−11 M (<10 parasites/µL), which allows its use in detecting malaria in its early stages. The sensitivity is higher than that of other traditional detection methods like laser desorption mass spectrometry and blood cell counting [ ]. 7.6. Aldolase In the study by Wang et al. 2014, the monoclonal antibody (mAb) 1C3-12 F10 pair was chosen from a number of clones that secrete anti-aldolase mAb and produced exclusively for detecting the P. vivax aldolase antigen. The mAb 1C3-12 F10 combination, which targets aldolase unique to P. vivax , demonstrated exceptional sensitivity and specificity of 97.4% and 100%, respectively. Additionally, 100% and 99.5% positive predictive values (PPV) and negative predictive values (NPV) were noted. The advantage of this method is that it was developed to specifically detect only the P. vivax aldolase antigen [ ]. 7.7. Conclusions and Future Perspectives Based on our discussion, we found that there are five biomarkers currently in use that are ideal for application in malaria detection methods, namely HRP2, pLDH, hemozoin, aldolase, and pGDH. Other biomarkers, such as CRP, Ang-1, Ang-2, and PCT, have the potential for malaria detection based on the possibility of differentiating malaria severity and determining the levels of these biomarkers in the body and comparing them with malaria parasitemia. However, several shortcomings still exist, such as a lack of sensitivity and specificity for Plasmodium . Biomarkers are still being developed that may possibly become ideal and specific biomarkers for malaria. Furthermore, RDTs have been developed for the five ideal malaria biomarkers. The advantages of RDT examination as a tool for rapid malaria diagnosis are that pathogen infection can be rapidly confirmed, there are no requirements for specialized knowledge and expensive equipment and the simplicity of the procedure. Regarding the type of samples used for malaria biomarker detection, blood samples are generally the most abundant and suitable. This is related to the erythrocytic infection stage of the malaria parasite’s life cycle, during which virulence factors are produced. Malaria biomarkers are also produced in infected red blood cells during this stage. Regarding currently applied methods for malaria detection, several have been developed from known biomarkers, where each biomarker gives different results in detection. This can be seen from the sensitivity and specificity resulting from the detection test. It is known that HRP2 when used as a biomarker, produces sensitive and specific results for P. falciparum . Such high sensitivity and specificity are the results of the HRP2 protein being unique to P. falciparum and therefore not found in other Plasmodium species. Regarding the pLDH biomarker, it is known that pLDH provides specific test results for various species of Plasmodium . The level of pLDH in blood is also correlated with the level of parasitemia. Hemozoin is produced in all parasite species, and hemozoin crystals are produced when parasites attack red blood cells whose contents are related to disease development. Therefore, hemozoin can be used as a biomarker for detecting various species of Plasmodium . However, there are currently limitations for determining which species of Plasmodium are detected from the test. There is still potential for further development and investigations regarding the Plasmodium species that can be detected based on hemozoin. Regarding its use as a biomarker, aldolase is known to allow sensitive and specific results for P. vivax detection. However, it has limited sensitivity if used for other Plasmodium species. Thus, it remains a challenge to obtain a specific and sensitive aldolase-based method for the detection of other Plasmodium species. Use of pGDH as a biomarker is based on this enzyme being found in all Plasmodium species. pGDH can provide specific test results for P. falciparum . CRP is a nonspecific biomarker and cannot be used to determine the species of Plasmodium . However, CRP can be used to assess whether levels are normal and compared with malaria parasitemia levels. Ang-1 and Ang-2 are known to have the potential for malaria detection based on increased cytoadherence of infected erythrocytes to the vascular endothelium. However, there are no studies demonstrating the detection of Ang-1 and Ang-2 in malaria. Thus, further research is needed to determine whether Ang-1 and Ang-2 may be considered ideal biomarkers for use in malaria detection. Regarding PCT, it was reported to be higher in severe malaria

Introduction Understanding the impact of early-life stressors is critical, given their enduring influence on health across the lifecourse, particularly cognitive functioning. Exposure to familial disruptions during childhood—such as parental divorce, separation, or death—has been consistently linked to adverse social, emotional, and physical outcomes that persist into adulthood (Donnelly et al., 2023; ). Emerging evidence further underscores the role of early family environments in shaping later-life psychosocial and cognitive well-being. For instance, emotionally distant family climates have been associated with greater loneliness and diminished sense of purpose in adulthood (Goeke-Morey et al., 2023), while childhood social isolation has been linked to poorer neuronal health in midlife (Barrett-Young et al., 2023). Disruptions in childhood environments during vulnerable developmental windows negatively influence cognitive domains such as episodic memory and processing speed, highlighting areas that may be particularly susceptible to early-life stress exposure (Nurmi et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2020). Conversely, there is evidence that high parental involvement in early life may protect against late-life cognitive decline, reinforcing how parental disruption can impact crucial psychosocial resources (Morita et al., 2021). Additionally, parental loss or divorce has been associated with increased risk of cognitive decline, potentially through disruptions to early social support systems and prolonged activation of stress-related physiological pathways ( ). For instance, examined the epigenetic consequences of early-life stressors by conducting genome-wide DNA methylation analyses in two large cohorts of middle-aged adults. DNA methylation plays a critical role in gene regulation within the central nervous system, and disruptions to methylation patterns—whether due to developmental mutations or environmental stressors—are frequently associated with impaired cognitive functioning ( ). identified nine differentially methylated regions in midlife that were significantly linked to cumulative early-life adversity, including stressors such as parental separation and parental death. Notably, the experience of parental death during childhood uniquely emerged as a driver of specific epigenetic alterations, highlighting that certain forms of parental disruption may have particularly pronounced biological implications for cognitive health across the life course. While epigenetic mechanisms represent one biological pathway, chronic stress in early life may accelerate cognitive aging and elevate dementia risk, in part through its effects on systemic inflammation ( ; ; ). Although inflammation serves an essential protective function, sustained systemic inflammation is increasingly recognized as a driver of adverse health outcomes (Majoka & Schimming, 2021). This chronic, low-grade inflammatory state, termed “inflammaging,” characterizes human aging and is a well-established risk factor associated with chronic diseases, disability, frailty, and mortality ( ; ). Of particular relevance to brain health, chronic systemic inflammation has been implicated in accelerated biological aging, neurodegenerative processes and reduced neuronal plasticity ( ; ; ; ). In large epidemiological studies, systemic inflammation is commonly assessed using biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) ( ). Importantly, these biological processes do not occur in a vacuum. Structural inequalities, such as racism, sexism, and economic injustice, are powerful macro-level determinants that exacerbate stress exposure and shape access to health-promoting resources across the lifespan ( ; Gee & Hicken, 2021). For example, economic inequality limits access to preventative care and amplifies exposure to psychosocial stressors, which in turn interact with physiological systems such as the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and contribute to chronic low-grade inflammation in aging ( ). Evidence from both animal models and human research supports the association between systemic inflammation and cognitive decline. For example, cohort studies from the Netherlands found that higher levels of inflammatory markers were associated with lower global cognitive performance and memory functioning, particularly among apolipoprotein E ε4 (APOE4) carriers, a genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (Schram et al., 2007). A recent systematic review further demonstrated that individuals with Alzheimer’s disease have elevated levels of inflammatory markers, including CRP and IL-6, compared to cognitively healthy controls (Childs et al., 2024). However, these findings are heterogeneous, as many studies suffer from small sample sizes, cross-sectional or short-term designs, and reliance on a single inflammatory marker. Few have examined inflammation’s impact on prodromal cognitive decline in mid- to late-life adults (Childs et al., 2024; Schram et al., 2007). Importantly, the specific mechanisms linking inflammation to cognitive impairment remain underexplored ( ). Although inflammation tends to increase with age, there is considerable interindividual variability in its trajectory. As such, examining psychosocial influences on inflammatory aging processes is essential to understanding differential risks for cognitive decline. For example, early-life adversity has been shown to prime microglia (i.e., the brain’s innate immune cells) to become hyperresponsive to later-life stressors and less effective in clearing amyloid deposits ( ; Singhaarachchi et al., 2024). The developing brain is particularly vulnerable to stress, and early adversity can result in long-term structural changes and persistent immune dysregulation (Singhaarachchi et al., 2024). Indeed, a recent review concluded that childhood adversity is associated with increased risk for developing Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias

Systemic inflammation may also rise during midlife due to hormonal shifts, particularly among women undergoing menopause. Declines in estrogen are associated with elevated inflammatory markers, which may partially account for the higher prevalence of ADRD among women (Childs et al., 2024; ; Nichols et al., 2022). Racially and ethnically minoritized individuals are more likely to experience early-life adversities such as parental divorce and death and may bear greater consequences due to factors like financial instability and limited access to supportive resources (Furstenberg et al., 1983; Smock et al., 2023; Sun & Li, 2007). Additionally, exposure to racism and discrimination is uniquely experienced by minoritized groups and has been associated with chronic stress responses and increased inflammation. For instance, a longitudinal study of women found that discrimination predicted higher CRP levels over seven years ( ). Analyses using the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) further show that the link between discrimination and health is mediated by systemic disadvantage, such as educational and occupational inequities ( ; ). Importantly, Black and Hispanic adults are at higher risk for Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias, even after adjusting for genetic factors, and consistently exhibit disparities in cognitive function and decline ( ; ). For example, data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study show that Black participants scored lower on episodic memory and executive function, partially explained by cumulative stress exposure ( ). Our study builds on limitations of prior work by examining early life adversity, inflammation, and cognitive function, since we are using a nationally representative sample of middle-aged and older adults, and are characterizing inflammation across multiple biomarkers. Drawing upon the approach developed by , we created a latent variable signifying systemic inflammation incorporating CRP, IL-6, IL-10, IL-1RA TNFR1, IGF-1, and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio. This allows for the more robust characterization of inflammation as derived from several biomarkers. Our primary aim is to explore whether systemic inflammation mediates the association between early-life parental disruption and late-life cognition. Secondarily, we aim to examine whether these pathways differ across racial/ethnic groups. Meier and colleagues’ research found that this latent variable of systemic inflammation predicts four-year mortality beyond other key risk factors such as multimorbidity and obesity. Given the established impact of systemic inflammation on brain health outcomes, it is plausible that inflammation may also play a significant mediating role in the relationship between early-life familial stressors (i.e., parental disruption) and cognitive decline. We hypothesize that early-life familial stressors are associated with greater cognitive decline in later life and this relationship is mediated by systemic inflammation. Additionally, we anticipate that these relationships may vary by ethnoracial group given disparate exposures to structural factors such as racism, sexism, and economic inequality. Methodology Data for this study were collected as part of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), a large, publicly-available, nationally representative dataset of adults in the United States over age 50 which collects data biennially. HRS data collection is overseen by the University of Michigan IRB, and de-identified public-use data files are released to researchers for secondary analysis. This dataset contains robust measures of cognitive health, systemic inflammation, and psychosocial factors relevant to this present study. Data for this study were aggregated from a variety of HRS data resources. Information about cognitive health was taken from the 2016 HRS Core Survey. The HRS Core survey is administered longitudinally to all HRS participants every two years. Data concerning systemic inflammation were drawn from the 2016 HRS Venous Blood Study (VBS; the only time point at which these blood-based biomarkers were collected), administered to consenting HRS respondents who neither required a proxy respondent nor resided in a nursing home at the time of data collection (Crimmins et al., 2025). Data about early life, including parental disruption, were aggregated from the 2015–2017 Life History Mail Survey (LHMS), a dataset that collects information about participants retrospectively allowing for a unique assessment of early life variables that may affect later life outcomes ( ). The HRS was approved by the University of Michigan’s Institutional Review Board (IRB), and all participants provided informed consent prior to participation. Variables Parental disruption. Data about early life parental disruption was assessed via three items: one asking about early life parental divorce, one asking about early life parental death, and one asking about early life separation from a parent, all before the age of 16. These items were taken from the LHMS. Participant answers were coded dichotomously (Yes to any item /No to all 3 items). Global cognition. Global cognition was assessed using the TICS, a cognitive screening test designed for phone administration, that includes items to assess orientation, attention, episodic memory, language and memory (Brandt et al., 1988). TICS scores ranged from 0 −27 where a higher score indicates greater cognitive function. Systemic inflammation. Systemic inflammation was estimated as a latent variable, using 7 observed blood-based biomarker indicators drawn from the HRS VBS. These included Interleukin-10 (log-transformed), Interleukin-6 (log-transformed), C-reactive protein (log-transformed), Tumor necrosis factor receptor-1 (log-transformed), Interleukin-1RA (log-transformed), Insulin-like growth factor-1 (log-transformed), and the proportion of neutrophils to lymphocytes (log-transformed) (Crimmins et al., 2025). Sample demographics. The primary moderator for the analysis was racial/ethnic identity (non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic of any race, other race/ethnicity). Additionally, analysis controlled for covariates including participant age (in years), gender (0= male, 1=female), educational attainment (0=less than HS degree, 1=HS degree/GED, 2=some college, 3=college degree, 4=education beyond college), total household wealth (in quintiles), employment status (0=employed, 1=not employed, 2=retired, 3=other), and marital status (0=married, 1=separated/divorced, 2=widowed, 3=never married). Additionally, we controlled for childhood sociodemographic confounders, including parental education (the greater of mother’s or father’s educational attainment in years), perceived relationship quality with parents before age 18 (mean-score average of relationship quality with mother and father before 18, ranging from 1 = lowest to 6 = highest), and self-reported family financial situation up until age 16 (0 =pretty well off financially, 1 = about average, 2 = poor, 3 = it varied). Statistical Analysis We utilized structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the relationship between early-life parental disruption, systemic inflammation, and cognition. SEM provides a robust analytical framework, enabling the simultaneous testing of direct and indirect effects while controlling for potential confounders. Moreover, it allows for the estimation of systemic inflammation as a latent measure, using a variety of blood-based inflammatory biomarkers as observed indicators. Specifically, we examined systemic inflammation as a mediator between early-life parental disruptions (divorce, death, or separation) and cognitive functioning in later life ( ). We assessed model fit using conventional indices, including comparative fit index (CFI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean residual (SRMR). Higher CFI values indicate better model fit, with values of 0.95 or above typically reflecting good fit. For RMSEA, values less than or equal to 0.06 are generally interpreted as indicating good model fit. Similarly, SRMR values lower than or equal to 0.08 are considered acceptable model fit ( ). The final SEM was stratified by race/ethnicity, due to significant differences across racial/ethnic groups concerning effects of interest. Sensitivity Analyses We conducted a series of sensitivity analyses to ensure the robustness of the findings. First sensitivity analysis explored the potential moderating effects of intersectional factors (i.e., gender and education), which showed non-significant results. Next, we examined whether our findings remained robust after including BMI as a covariate, and this did not weaken our main results ( ). Then we tested two additional models with different operationalization of the parental disruption measure: a model with sum score of parental disruption ( ) and type-specific parental disruption model ( ). According to these analyses, parental death was a primary driver of the differential findings across ethnoracial groups. That is, the effect of parental death on cognition through inflammation was only significant among non-Hispanic Whites. Discussion This study examined how early-life parental disruption relates to late-life cognition via systemic inflammation and whether these pathways differ across ethnoracial groups. Our findings indicate that systemic inflammation partially mediates the association between early-life parental disruption stressors and cognitive functioning—but only among non-Hispanic White participants. Inflammation was directly associated with poorer cognitive functioning for both non-Hispanic White and Hispanic participants, but not for Black participants. Notably, while non-Hispanic Black participants reported the highest rates of early-life parental disruption, this adversity was not significantly associated with systemic inflammation or cognition in this group. These results underscore the need to better understand sociocultural and structural factors that may shape vulnerability and resilience in cognitive aging. The finding that systemic inflammation was associated with lower cognitive performance in non-Hispanic White and Hispanic participants but not in Black participants aligns with prior research showing heterogeneous effects of inflammation on cognitive aging across racial/ethnic groups ( ). One possibility is that differential exposure to cumulative stress and socioeconomic disadvantage may alter the role that inflammation plays in cognitive aging. While Black participants generally had higher mean levels of inflammatory markers, their cognitive outcomes may be shaped more directly by other chronic structural burdens, such as income volatility, discrimination, or reduced access to quality education and healthcare. These persistent stressors may have a more pervasive impact on cognition than transient inflammation alone. It is also possible that racialized coping mechanisms or community-level resilience factors buffer the neurocognitive impact of inflammation among Black individuals. For example, research has shown that Black adults often exhibit stronger religious or familial social support, which may serve as protective psychosocial buffers. Alternatively, systemic racism may produce a chronic “wear and tear” effect on multiple physiological systems, meaning that cognitive outcomes are already affected via non-inflammatory mechanisms ( ). As such, inflammation may not add appreciable explanatory value in this group ( ; ). That early-life parental disruption was significantly associated with inflammation, and that inflammation mediated its relationship with cognition only among non-Hispanic White participants is a particularly important and novel finding. Sensitivity analyses indicated that this pathway was largely driven by parental death. Consistent with our findings, reported that parental death predicts late-life cognitive impairment in the HRS, particularly when losses occur earlier in the life course. In contrast to our results, they observed no significant racial/ethnic differences in this association. Our findings suggest that systemic inflammation may be one pathway linking bereavement to cognition primarily among non-Hispanic White individuals, with other mechanisms serving as the dominant drivers in other groups. Consistent with our findings, reported that parental death predicts late-life cognitive impairment in the HRS, particularly when losses occur earlier in the life course. In contrast to our results, they observed no significant racial/ethnic differences in this association. Our findings suggest that systemic inflammation may be one pathway linking bereavement to cognition primarily among non-Hispanic White individuals, with other mechanisms serving as the dominant drivers in other groups. This could reflect differences in the meaning or impact of early-life family stressors across cultural or social contexts. For example, parental divorce or death may represent a more significant rupture in perceived life stability for non-Hispanic White participants, particularly in the absence of extended kin networks or collectivist cultural norms seen in some Hispanic or Black communities, or when these adverse experiences occur earlier in life ( ; ; ). In contrast, among Black and Hispanic families, structural adversity may be more normalized or buffered by broader community ties, resulting in different physiological or emotional responses ( ; ). Another possibility is that non-Hispanic White participants may underreport cumulative stressors or lack compensatory resilience factors, making discrete early-life events like parental disruption more salient in their long-term biological risk profiles. In contrast, among Black and Hispanic participants, early adversity may be one among many chronic stress exposures and may not independently drive long-term inflammation in a detectable way. These patterns also raise important questions about measurement equivalence—both in how early-life stress is reported and how inflammation is experienced and interpreted biologically across groups. While we used a latent variable approach to model inflammation, it remains possible that these markers behave differently due to genetic, environmental, or epigenetic factors that vary by population. Furthermore, these markers may vary in their specific associations with cognitive and other health outcomes, an important area for future research. This study highlights the importance of addressing structural determinants of health when designing interventions aimed at preventing cognitive decline. While systemic inflammation appears to be a relevant biological mechanism for some groups, other structural and psychosocial pathways—such as chronic stress exposure, educational disadvantage, and systemic discrimination—must also be addressed. Policies that improve early-life environments, enhance access to preventive care, and reduce socioeconomic inequality may help mitigate long-term risk across all groups, but especially among those with disproportionate exposure to adversity. Moreover, interventions to promote cognitive resilience may need to be tailored by group. For instance, enhancing educational quality and socioeconomic stability may be especially protective for Black individuals, consistent with prior research indicating that SES factors can attenuate racial disparities in cognitive aging ( ). Key strengths of this study include its use of a large, nationally representative dataset, the integration of life course data across multiple HRS modules, and the application of a robust, latent construct of systemic inflammation derived from multiple biomarkers. However, several limitations should be noted. First, early-life stressors were retrospectively reported, which may introduce recall bias. However, we are less concerned in this context given the salience of the events assessed. Parental death, divorce, and separation are specific, objective and highly memorable life disruptions, and prior research indicates that such events are typically recalled with greater reliability than more routine or ambiguous experiences ( ). Second, subgroup sample sizes were smaller for Hispanic and Black participants, which may have limited statistical power to detect more subtle effects. Third, biomarkers were assessed at a single time point, limiting our ability to capture temporal dynamics of inflammation. Future research should explore intersectional factors (e.g., urbanicity, class, and sexuality) to better understand nuanced patterns of risk and resilience in cognitive aging. Longitudinal models that incorporate changes in inflammation and cognition over time, as well as qualitative data to contextualize early-life adversity, would further illuminate these pathways. Additionally, further exploration of culturally grounded coping strategies and community-level protective factors may help explain group differences in the observed pathways. Conclusion This study provides evidence that early-life parental disruption is associated with late-life cognitive function through systemic inflammation—but only among non-Hispanic White adults. Despite higher rates of familial stressors among Black and Hispanic participants, these pathways did not emerge as significant, underscoring the importance of sociocultural context, structural inequities, and cumulative adversity in shaping cognitive aging. Our findings suggest that systemic inflammation may not be a universal biological mechanism linking early stress to cognitive decline. Instead, the impact of early-life adversity appears to vary by ethnoracial group, likely reflecting intersecting effects of socioeconomic disadvantage, resilience resources, and lived experiences of structural oppression. These results call for more nuanced, equity-focused approaches in cognitive aging research and policy. Interventions that aim to reduce systemic inflammation may be effective for some populations, but broader strategies that dismantle structural barriers and promote educational, economic, and psychosocial support are essential to promoting brain health across diverse communities. Introduction Transgender and gender non-binary (TGNB) individuals are disproportionally affected by HIV ( ). In 2017, transgender individuals were 3 times more likely than the national average to have a new HIV diagnosis ( ), with HIV prevalence 19 times higher for transgender women compared to cisgender women ages 15–49 years old ( ). Among all adults and adolescents, 92% of diagnoses of HIV infections in transgender individuals were among transgender women ( ). Approximately 1 in 7 (14%) transgender women in the US are estimated to be living with HIV ( ). Disparities in HIV in the TGNB community are even more pronounced within ethnic and racial minority sub-populations. In 2018, 40% of new HIV diagnoses in transgender men and 49% of new HIV diagnoses in transgender women were among Black individuals, higher than any other racial/ethnic group ( ). Although prevalence data specific to adolescent transgender individuals of color are limited, recent HIV rates from a meta-analysis of adults estimated 44% of Black transgender women and 26% of Hispanic/Latina transgender women are living with HIV ( ). In order to decrease the incidence of new HIV infection in adolescents and young adults (AYA), an emphasis on effective HIV prevention strategies is essential. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a highly effective medication for reducing the risk of acquiring HIV when taken consistently and is recommended for individuals at increased risk for infection ( ). PrEP has been well studied and FDA approved in adolescents ( , ). A 2019 systematic review of 14 randomized control trials, 8 observational studies, and 7 studies of diagnostic accuracy demonstrated a 75% reduction in risk of HIV infection comparing PrEP with placebo when there was a high adherence to PrEP ( ). However, while more than 20% of new HIV infections occur among AYA, this population accounted for less than 10% of all PrEP prescriptions in 2017 ( ). Despite their higher need for HIV prevention services, little research is available regarding PrEP awareness and engagement among TGNB AYA, although preliminary research has identified some of the barriers to PrEP care. A recent study of 202 TGNB AYA aged 15–24 found an overall high level of PrEP awareness, but little specific knowledge regarding PrEP. While only 0.5% of respondents were using PrEP, over half of those who had heard of PrEP prior to the study were willing to use it ( ). Other studies have shown that many sexual and gender minority adolescents assigned male at birth are not aware of PrEP, and many do not know how they could access PrEP if needed ( ). A focus group study of adult TGNB participants identified limited healthcare access, mental health problems, potential drug interactions with gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT), and lack of protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) as barriers to starting PrEP ( ). It is also known that TGNB individuals face disproportionally higher rates of discrimination and stigma in general as well as within medicine, which has resulted in limited use of medical services, including HIV prevention ( ). The PrEP care continuum provides a framework for the multiple steps needed to maintain awareness, uptake, adherence, and retention in care ( ). In this study, we evaluated PrEP awareness, utilization and preferences as well as perceived barriers to PrEP among TGNB AYAs who seek care in a gender-affirming care clinic. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate PrEP awareness and current utilization among TGNB adolescents and young adults. The secondary objectives of this study were to assess PrEP preferences among TGNB adolescents and young adults and to determine perceived barriers to PrEP usage among TGNB adolescents and young adults. Participants were recruited from seven gender-affirming care clinics in the United States at the following institutions: University of California San Diego, Rady Children's Hospital, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago, Children's Hospital Los Angeles, Oregon Health and Science University Hospital, and West Virginia University Medicine Children's Hospital. This study recruited from seven clinics in five states housed within academic medical centers in the United States. Clinic sizes ranged from 1 to 15 providers and all routinely prescribed PrEP. Patient population size ranged from 400 to 3,500 patients, and the majority served a predominantly urban population with one clinic serving a rural population. All participating gender-affirming care clinics provided PrEP. To be eligible to participate in the study, individuals needed to be: 15–24 years old, self-identified as transgender or non-binary, English-speaking, and receiving care in a gender-affirming clinic. TGNB youth were passively recruited between December 2021 and November 2022 using flyers posted in waiting rooms and other clinical spaces. Participants scanned a QR code on the flyer using their smart phone and were directed to the online consent form and survey. The online survey was created using questions adapted from a randomized control trial specific to transgender AYA ( ). The questions were initially developed by a measures harmonization group at the Adolescent Medicine Trials Network for HIV Intervention and adapted to fit the needs of our patient population by adjusting the language within the question and shortening the answer choice options to allow for faster completion of survey. The survey contained 26 items, including questions assessing sociodemographic factors, hormone therapy use, sexual risk behaviors and STI history, PrEP awareness, PrEP use and accessibility, perceptions of PrEP, PrEP preferences, willingness to use PrEP, and barriers to use ( ). Questions 1 through 11 assessed sociodemographic factors including: age, location, sex assigned at birth, gender identity, ethnicity, race, primary language, highest level of education, employment status, housing status, and insurance status. To assess GAHT usage participants were asked a dichotomous yes/no question: “Are you currently on hormone therapy as part of gender-affirming care?”. If the respondent answered yes, they were diverted to a multiple-choice question to assess the type of hormone therapy. We then asked participants “If yes to the previous question, how do you take hormone therapy?” and they were given the options: pills, injectables, gels, patches, and other. To assess sexual risk behaviors and STI history participants were asked 5 dichotomous yes/no questions with the option to also choose “prefer not to disclose”. Sexual activity was defined as penetrative anal, penetrative vaginal, or oral sex in the last 12 months. The remainder of the survey was considered “Section 2”; which started with an informative description of PrEP (see ). To asses PrEP awareness, participants were asked “Before today, have you ever heard of people regularly taking anti-HIV medicines BEFORE a sexual or drug use exposure, to reduce the risk of getting HIV? This is called pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP.” Responses were obtained on a likert scale with 1–5 responses ranging from “No, I’ve never heard of it before today” to “Yes, I know a lot about it.” and participants were given the option to “decline to answer”. If participants chose any answer choice that started with “Yes, […]” or “decline to answer” they were directed to questions 17 and 18 which assessed PrEP accessibility and use. This was assessed by asking the following multiple-choice questions “In the past 3 months have you talked to a medical provider about starting PrEP?” and “Have you ever been prescribed PrEP by a healthcare provider? (regardless of whether you took it or not)”. Responses were on a likert scale with 1–5 responses “Yes, and we both thought it was right for me and I should start Prep” to “No, I have never spoken to a provider about starting PrEP.” For the latter responses we used multiple choice and included “Yes, I am on PrEP right now”, “Yes, I was in the past, but I’m not on PrEP anymore”, and “No, I’ve never been prescribed PrEP”. If a participant indicated they had been on PrEP in the past they were directed to question 20. This question assessed accessibility to PrEP by asking the following multiple choice question [select all that apply]: “Did you get your PrEP from the following people or places?”. The options included “Doctor or other health care provider”, “Sex partner”, “Friend”, “Relative”, “Acquaintance”, “Internet”, “Decline to answer”, and a short answer option. However, there may be other ways you can take PrEP in the future that are also effective at preventing HIV. How would you prefer to take PrEP if other options were available?”. Multiple choice answer options included: “As a pill I take every day”, “As an on-demand pill (around when I have sex–that is, 2 pills 2–24 h before sex, 1 pill 24 h after the first dose, and 1 pill 24 h after the second dose)”, “As an injection that I get from my provider every 2 months”, “As an injection that I get from my provider every 6 months”, and “As an implant that is placed under my skin once a year”. The final survey question assessed reasons for PrEP non-use, participants were asked “What are your reasons for not starting PrEP?” Participants were given 21 different reasons one might not start PrEP and instructed to identify up to three reasons they have not started PrEP. This extensive list was generated based on prior studies of adolescents in parallel age range, including data from TGNB and MSM individuals ( , – ). Participants were de-identified, and once they completed the survey, they were emailed a $10 electronic gift card. We reviewed completed surveys to identify possible repeat participation by the same participant based on IP addresses, duration to complete the survey, and similar responses. Those that were concerning for duplicates were excluded. We determined the minimal plausible amount of time for survey completion by participants was 1.5 min given the survey was 26 questions and 50% of participants took over 5 min to complete the survey; we concluded that participants who spent less than 1.5 min to complete survey would be omitted from the results. IP addresses were used to minimize fraudulent responses, but allowing one IP address to be utilized twice if it was linked to two separate email addresses and met all other criteria. This was allowed in the event two different participants used the same device to complete the survey. Straightlining is the tendency of survey respondents to select the same response multiple times in a line of answers on a survey. To avoid straightlining participants were presented with one question per page, they were required to answer each question prior to proceeding, and matrix grid questions were avoided wherever possible. Based on these criteria, 22 survey responses were omitted from the study. Quantitative analysis examined the differences in PrEP awareness and preferences. The data analysis for this study was performed using Qualtrics software, Version XM. Nonparametric test of proportion, the independent Chi-squared test was used, with the level of significance set at 0.05. The study was approved by the University of California San Diego Institutional Review Board. Parental consent was not required for minors given the low-risk nature of the study. Most participants were in high school (51.3%) and had stable housing (82.1%). Just over half (51%) were currently on gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT). Regarding their sexual history, 70 (45%) participants had been sexually active within the last 12 months, and 95% had never been diagnosed with an STI. Thirty-three percent of 15–19 year olds had oral sex in the last 12 months and 21% had vaginal sex in the past 12 months. The majority (70%) had never been tested for HIV ( ). Prep awareness 104 participants (67%) had heard of PrEP prior to completing the survey. Of the 70 participants who had been sexually active in the last 12 months, 69% had previously heard of PrEP. Participants who identified as non-Hispanic/Latino were more likely to have heard of PrEP compared to Hispanic/Latino individuals, (73% vs. 53%, p = 0.016 ) ( ). There were no differences in PrEP awareness by age, gender identity, geographic region, insurance status or sexual activity ( ). Prep access and use Of those participants who had heard of PrEP prior to the study, only 12% had spoken to a medical provider about starting PrEP in the past 3 months, 3% had been prescribed PrEP in the past and 4% were currently taking PrEP. Of the participants who had a history of sexual activity, 17% had spoken to a healthcare provider about PrEP. Of the 7 patients who had previously or were currently taking PrEP, 5 received PrEP from a health care provider, 1 participant received PrEP from a relative and 1 obtained PrEP from the internet. Of the 99 participants who had never been prescribed PrEP, most (61%) reported knowing of a medical provider that would prescribe PrEP to them. Prep perceptions and preferences Participants not currently on PrEP were asked if they thought PrEP was right for them. Seventy-eight (51%) reported they were not sure, and only 5 (3%) thought PrEP was right for them. When asked if they would take PrEP if they could get it for free, 54 (36%) reported they would take it; when asked if they would take PrEP if it was free and without their parent's knowledge this increased to 66 (44%). Of the participants who did not think they needed PrEP, nearly half (47%) reported a history of sexual activity in the past 12 months, 4% had a history of STI diagnosis in their lifetime, and 32% had been tested for HIV in their lifetime. There were no statistically significant differences in the preference for route of administration of PrEP based on type of GAHT used based on chi-squared test of independence. Participants on both oral (11/14, 79%) and injectable (29/42, 69%) GAHT preferring to take oral PrEP (See ). Willingness and barriers to use PrEP When asked if they planned to start taking PrEP, 15 (10%) participants reported they were planning to start taking PrEP. The most frequently cited reason for not starting PrEP endorsed by 92 (61%) participants was not thinking they needed it. Other common reasons for not starting PrEP included not being aware of PrEP previously, worries about forgetting to take it, interactions with GAHT, financial coverage, side effects, not knowing where to get PrEP, long term effects of PrEP, needing parental permission, and stigma (See ). Discussion This anonymous online survey study suggests that the majority of TGNB AYA who are followed at gender-affirming health clinics are aware of PrEP; however, few had been prescribed or were currently taking PrEP. These findings are similar to prior studies regarding PrEP awareness and use in TGNB AYA ( , , ). Many participants remained hesitant to start PrEP, with the main reason being they did not think they needed it. Our data showed just under half of the participants who did not think they needed PrEP reported a history of sexual activity in the last three months; however, this information alone does not necessarily place these patients at higher risk for HIV and we are unable to postulate the HIV risk in this sample. To determine if a patient should be started on PrEP it would be relevant to obtain information on barrier contraception, if they have been diagnosed with an STI in the past 6 months, HIV status of partners, injection drug use history, and post-exposure prophylaxis use which were not obtained in this study. This finding does underscore the importance of speaking with AYA confidentially and obtaining a sexual history, discussing sexual health behaviors that are associated with the risk of HIV acquisition, and introducing the topic of PrEP as recommended by the CDC for all sexually active individuals ( , , ). Further, of participants who

should be started on PrEP it would be relevant to obtain information on barrier contraception, if they have been diagnosed with an STI in the past 6 months, HIV status of partners, injection drug use history, and post-exposure prophylaxis use which were not obtained in this study. This finding does underscore the importance of speaking with AYA confidentially and obtaining a sexual history, discussing sexual health behaviors that are associated with the risk of HIV acquisition, and introducing the topic of PrEP as recommended by the CDC for all sexually active individuals ( , , ). Further, of participants who had never been prescribed PrEP, nearly 40% reported not knowing of a medical provider to prescribe them PrEP which is relevant given all gender-affirming health clinics who participated in the survey offering PrEP. These findings together emphasize the need for patient and healthcare provider education as well as provider responsibility to initiate these conversations. TGNB AYA who identified as Hispanic/Latinx were less likely to be aware of PrEP than their non-Hispanic/Latinx counterparts, consistent with the 2019 National HIV Prevention Program Monitoring and Evaluation HIV testing data which showed that PrEP awareness among Hispanic persons was lower compared with non-Hispanic persons ( ). Expanding culturally appropriate PrEP educational efforts is a key step to eliminating this disparity and reducing the impact of HIV on this community ( ). Research studies encompassing a larger Hispanic/Latinx population are critical to better understanding how to specifically address these topics in this community. Participants also noted not starting PrEP due to financial concern. Most of this patient population had private or public health insurance; while many insurers may cover PrEP it is unclear what co-pay the respondent may be responsible for and this may still pose a financial barrier to the respondent. Furthermore, given the age range of participants, some may have been on their parents' insurance plan which may require disclosure to a parent to obtain. Although few individuals reported they would take PrEP, many said they would take it if it was free and even more would take PrEP if it was free and without their parent's knowledge. Similar concerns have been reported in prior studies of cisgender sexual minority adolescents ( ). This increase in willingness to take PrEP suggests that many individuals are interested in taking PrEP, but financial and confidentiality-related barriers may be preventing them from starting the medication. Nearly all public and private insurers cover PrEP. In instances where a patient is uninsured or whose insurance does not cover PrEP medication, there are programs available to provide PrEP for free; however most are only available to adults ( ). Financial counseling is an important step to ensure successful PrEP uptake, persistence, and preventing barriers to care. While PrEP has been FDA approved for adolescents, each state's minor consent laws may impact access for adolescents including being able to confidentially obtain PrEP ( , ). Similar to what has been found in other studies ( ), participants were concerned about the possibility of drug interactions with their GAHT. This hesitation to start PrEP would require a multimodal approach to impact behavioral change in this population. Educating AYA on studies that have shown PrEP medications do not impact the effect of GAHT could be an important way to begin this conversation ( – ). Most participants preferred to take PrEP as an oral daily tablet over a longer acting injectable/implant or on demand tablet, which was a surprising finding given many used injectable GAHT. Among other variables, it is possible that they were more familiar with oral PrEP given it was the only FDA approved option prior to December 2021. Within one study, interviews among trans women on GAHT revealed they were concerned that they would need to be physically present in clinic to receive injectable PrEP and would only want to use injectable PrEP if they could inject it themselves ( ). Limitations of this study include that it may not represent all TGNB AYA given the relatively small sample size. The surveys were only distributed at pediatric gender health clinics affiliated with large university health systems and thus focused on individuals with reasonable access to medical care and potentially higher health literacy compared to individuals not being followed by a physician in a gender health clinic. Individuals were required to have access to a smart phone to complete the survey, and it was only available in English. In addition, the population's demographics differed in our study compared to those of the target population based on the 2014 CDC's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) ( ). The percentage of Black (non-Hispanic) individuals in our sample (4%) is notably lower than the estimated target population from the BRFSS (15%). A significant limitation given the potentially unique experiences of this population.

Although convenience sample data have contributed significantly to our understanding of the transgender population, these differences highlight its potential biases. The underrepresentation of black participants in our survey study can be attributed to a combination of factors including institutional and structural racism, geographic distribution of our clinics, and socio-economic factors affecting access to gender-affirming care. Future research engaging patients outside of university affiliated gender health clinics could aid in reaching these populations and should explore more inclusive recruitment strategies to address these limitations; including culturally congruent research processes, benefits of participation, and altruism toward and involvement of family or community ( ). Our survey was distributed at gender health centers in large metropolitan regions notably located in states with less restrictive laws on access to gender affirming care; thus many states with more restrictive laws are not represented in this sample. We acknowledge that while strategies were utilized to minimize fraudulent responses there were other ways in which fraudulent responses could have been missed and still included in the study given our inability to use advanced technology to stop a participant from completing repeated attempts of survey from different IP addresses. This method was not used due to funding limitations. Given that many of the questions were based on the same rating scale, there could have been some non-differentiation in ratings that contributed to fraudulent responses. Due to limitations in the duration of the study and prioritization of high value questions to avoid survey fatigue, we did not obtain detailed information regarding facilitators of PrEP uptake as well as specific HIV risk such as barrier precautions, history of STIs and partner status to determine the HIV risk of each individual. Future research should specifically include this valuable information. Our study underscores the need for broad PrEP educational efforts for both TGNB AYA and their healthcare providers to improve knowledge, identify potential PrEP candidates among TGNB AYA at risk for HIV infection and improve access by addressing identified barriers. Many of the reasons obtained in this study for not taking PrEP are common misconceptions which can be addressed with AYA during medical visits. These findings should inform clinical practice for healthcare providers with an emphasis on ensuring patients are aware of PrEP, helping them obtain PrEP, and addressing common concerns for not starting PrEP. Future studies examining reasons for slow uptake of PrEP as well as engaging Black and Latinx TGNB AYA to develop interventions for PrEP engagement are needed.

Introduction Muco-obstructive lung diseases, including cystic fibrosis (CF), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), primary ciliary dyskinesia, and non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis, are characterized by intrapulmonary mucus accumulation, airway inflammation, and microbial infections – . CF is caused by mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator ( Cftr ) gene and currently affects an estimated 100,000 people worldwide , . CF lung disease, a result of single ion channel defect, involves airway surface liquid (ASL) dehydration, mucin hypersecretion, mucostasis, and mucus obstruction . These muco-obstructive features are associated with chronic airway inflammation and recurrent microbial infections . However, our understanding of how various molecules identified in the CF patients or CF animal models are involved in the pathogenesis of CF-like muco-obstructive lung disease remains unclear. High mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) is a highly conserved non-histone chromatin-associated protein , . Under normal physiological conditions, HMGB1 performs essential functions within the nucleus, ensuring chromatin stability and regulating transcription . However, during inflammatory conditions, HMGB1 is released into the extracellular milieu where it acts as a danger/damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) . HMGB1 is known to ligate with Toll-like receptor (TLR)-2, TLR-4, and receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) , . Notably, elevated levels of HMGB1 have been reported in multiple clinical studies and animal models of lung diseases, including muco-obstructive lung diseases, such as CF – . According to previous reports, HMGB1 can play a protective role in lung injury and bacterial infection , . However, the role of HMGB1 in the pathogenesis of CF-like lung diseases remains unclear. The sodium channel nonvoltage-gated 1 , beta subunit ( Scnn1b )-transgenic (Tg+) mice, which overexpress β subunit of epithelial Na + channel (ENaC) in airway epithelial cells , have increased epithelial Na + absorption that results in ASL dehydration, impaired mucociliary clearance (MCC), airway mucus obstruction, mucous cell metaplasia (MCM), airway inflammation, and spontaneous bacterial infections – . To reduce extracellular release of HMGB1 into the airspaces, we previously introduced airway epithelial cell-specific HMGB1 deficiency in Scnn1b -Tg+ (Tg+) mice, a model of human cystic fibrosis (CF)-like lung diseases . While the deletion of airway epithelial cell-specific HMGB1 did not reduce BALF HMGB1 levels, the intracellular HMGB1 deficiency resulted in exaggerated inflammatory responses . In the present study, we hypothesized that myeloid cell-derived HMGB1 deficiency will reduce extracellular HMGB1 levels in the lung airspaces of Tg+ mice, which will modulate pathological features of lung disease. To test this hypothesis, we evaluated the effect of myeloid cell-specific HMGB1 deficiency on various mucoinflammatory features of Tg+ mice. This study revealed that the myeloid cell-specific HMGB1 deficiency results in exaggerated inflammatory responses, excessive mucoobstruction, and unexpectedly, an improved bacterial clearance. BALF collection and analyses Mice were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of 2,2,2-tribromoethanol (Avertin, Millipore Sigma, Burlington, MA) and then euthanized by exsanguination via severing posterior vena cava. BALF was collected aseptically, and both total cell counts and differential cell counts were determined as previously reported , . Briefly, BALF from the right lung lobes was collected through lavaging with calcium- and magnesium- free Dulbecco’s Phosphate Buffered Saline (DPBS) (21-031-CV, Corning, Manassas, VA) using a weight-adjusted formula [mouse weight (g) × 0.0175 ml = ml DPBS instilled] . This procedure was performed twice by gently injecting and retrieving the calculated volume of DPBS . Cell pellets obtained after centrifugation of harvested BALF at 1000 × g for 5 min at 4 °C were resuspended in 500 µl of DPBS. Cell-free supernatant was frozen at -80°C for further analyses. Total cell counts were determined using a hemocytometer. Cytospin slides were prepared from 200 µl of cell pellets using a Statspin Cytofuge 2 (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA) and stained with modified Wright-Giemsa Stain (Newcomer Supply, Middleton, WI). The proportions of four key immune cells, i.e., macrophages, neutrophils, eosinophils, and lymphocytes, were determined by counting 200 cells per cytospin slide. Cytokines and chemokines were measured in cell-free BALF by a Luminex-XMAP-based assay (MCYTOMAG-70 K; EMD Millipore, Billerica, MA) and a BioPlex Pro Mouse Chemokine panel (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA), according to the manufacturer’s instructions and as reported previously . The entire list of cytokines and chemokines is included in Supplementary Table 1. Western blotting Equal protein amounts from BALF cell lysate or equal volumes of BALF were loaded on the NuPAGE 4–12% Bis-Tris gradient gel (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA) for electrophoresis. The gel was then subjected to PVDF membrane transfer using iBlot™ gel transfer device (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA) and the membrane was incubated with primary antibody. Rabbit polyclonal HMGB1 antibody (ab18256; Abcam, Cambridge, MA) was used as the primary antibody. For western blotting analyses of HMGB1 in BALF-derived cells, α-tubulin was used as a loading control using a mouse monoclonal primary antibody (T5168; Sigma-Aldrich, Burlington, MA). . IRDye 680RD goat anti-rabbit IgG (926-68071; LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE) and IRDye 800CW goat anti-mouse IgG (926-32210; LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE) secondary antibodies were used for HMGB1 and a-tubulin proteins, respectively. For western blotting analyses of HMGB1 in cell-free BALF, equal volumes of BALF were loaded into each well of the gel. The resulting data obtained were considered normalized to the body weights, as lavage volumes were calculated based on the individual body weights of mice. Immunostained protein bands were visualized using Odyssey CLx, Imager (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE) and quantified using the Fiji software . Immunohistochemistry (IHC) Immunostaining of HMGB1 was conducted on paraffin-embedded lung sections using rabbit polyclonal HMGB1 antibody (ab18256; Abcam, Cambridge, MA) as described previously . Mean linear intercept (MLI) measurements To measure the MLI, evenly-spaced vertical and horizontal test lines of defined length were placed on the chosen area of a lung section image . MLI was calculated by dividing the total length of the drawn line by the numbers of the septal intercepts along the line and averaging this intercept length value across measurements , . Myeloid cell-specific HMGB1 deletion induces elevated levels of inflammatory mediators in the lung airspaces of Tg+ mice Cytokines and chemokines play critical roles in the recruitment of immune cells , . Therefore, we assessed BALF levels of selected cytokines and chemokines that are relevant to immune cell recruitment. Myeloid cell-specific HMGB1 deletion leads to enhanced bacterial clearance in the airspaces of Tg+ mice The Tg+ mice are susceptible to spontaneous bacterial infection during the early postnatal period . To determine whether myeloid cell-specific HMGB1 deletion affects spontaneous bacterial clearance of Tg+ juvenile mice, we aseptically harvested BALF from all the four groups of mice and enumerated the colony-forming units (CFUs). Discussion Airway surface liquid layer dehydration in Tg+ mice results in airway mucus obstruction, mucous cell metaplasia (MCM), persistent neutrophilic airway inflammation, transient eosinophilic airway inflammation, and emphysema . Transcriptomic and exosomal proteomic analyses of WT and Tg+ airspaces reveal differential enrichment of numerous genes and protein signatures that indicate their roles in exaggerated inflammatory responses , . It is unclear whether the differentially-expressed genes or differentially-enriched proteins observed in Tg+ mice are actively contributing to the pathogenesis or if they are simply bystanders without a direct role in the pathological process. Therefore, functional studies are necessary to determine the precise role of these genes and proteins in disease manifestation. HMGB1 levels are elevated in the sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) of CF patients and cystic fibrosis mice models , – . In our previous study, we reported that the airway epithelial cell-specific deletion of HMGB1 in Tg+ mice results in heightened inflammatory responses and impaired clearance of spontaneous bacterial infection, without affecting mucus obstruction or airway epithelial remodeling. Interestingly, the BALF HMGB1 levels were not reduced in Tg+ mice with airway epithelial cell-specific HMGB1 deficiency . These findings suggested that the effects observed in the airway epithelial cell-specific HMGB1-deficient Tg+ mice were attributed to the intracellular role of HMGB1 in airway epithelial cells. Therefore, to continue our investigation on the role of extracellular HMGB1 on Tg+ lung disease, we compared HMGB1 protein levels in immune cells harvested from WT and Tg+ mice and found significantly elevated levels in Tg+ mice compared with WT mice (Fig. A). Therefore, we hypothesized that the HMGB1 released from myeloid cell contributes to the increased levels in BALF from Tg+ mice compared with WT mice. To test our hypothesis, we generated myeloid cell-specific HMGB1-deficient Tg+ mice and compared various features of Tg+ lung disease with HMGB1-sufficient Tg+ mice. Here, we addressed the following questions: (1) Does myeloid cell-specific HMGB1 deficiency affect lung inflammation, i.e., immune cell infiltration and levels of pro-inflammatory mediators in Tg+ airspaces? (2) Does myeloid cell-specific HMGB1 deletion affect airway mucus obstruction and MCM in Tg+ mice? (3) Does deficiency of myeloid cell-derived HMGB1 affect pulmonary pathology in Tg+ mice? (4) Does myeloid cell-specific HMGB1 deficiency compromise bacterial clearance in Tg+ airways? Extracellular HMGB1 treatment of the bronchial epithelial cells has been shown to upregulate mRNA and protein expression of two main gel-forming mucins MUC5AC and MUC5B . It remains unclear how myeloid cell-specific deletion of HMGB1 results in exaggerated airway mucus obstruction. We speculate that the hyperconcentration of ASL due to excessive cellular recruitment and deposition of their products, such as neutrophil extracellular traps, contributes to exaggerated mucus obstruction. The protease/antiprotease imbalance towards increased protease levels is implicated in the pathogenesis of emphysema – . For example, neutrophil and macrophage proteases has been shown to contribute to cigarette smoke-induced alveolar space enlargement, an indicator of emphysematous change, in mice , . Trojanek et al., demonstrated that matrix metalloproteinase 12 (MMP12) released from activated macrophages in Tg+ lungs contributes to alveolar wall destruction . Gehrig et al., reported that the deletion of neutrophil elastase in Tg+ mice mitigates alveolar space enlargement . Based on these reports, it appears that the HMGB1 deletion in myeloid cells induced macrophage activation and neutrophil recruitment, which likely through production of proteases and elastases, contributed to alveolar space enlargement in Tg+ mice. Another hallmark of Tg+ lung disease is the occurrence of spontaneous bacterial infections during early postnatal age, which are effectively cleared during early adulthood . Previous reports have suggested multiple host defense mechanisms that may influence spontaneous bacterial infections. For instance, elevated BALF neutrophil and macrophage counts, classical activation of macrophages, increased IgA levels in BALF, and reduced IL-10 levels have been reported to correlate with efficient bacterial clearance , – , , – . On the other hand, lack of innate lymphoid system, higher degree of mucus obstruction, and exposure to external agents (SHS, Ozone) have resulted in compromised bacterial clearance , , . Our data indicate that HMGB1 deletion in myeloid cells significantly increased bacterial clearance in Tg+ mice, which is likely attributable to the morphological activation of macrophages and increased neutrophilic recruitment. The current study also leaves several intriguing questions unanswered including: 1) Does myeloid cell-specific HMGB1 deletion affect pathological features of mucoinflammatory lung disease in mice during early neonatal and late adulthood stages? (2) What are other cellular sources of HMGB1 in Tg+ airspaces? 3) Whether myeloid cell-derived HMGB1 plays its role through molecular interactions with other proteins in airspaces of Tg+ mice? and 4) Whether the altered responses observed in myeloid cell-specific HMGB1-deficient Tg+ mice are driven by the loss of HMGB1 in a specific myeloid cell subtype? Further investigations are warranted to address these questions. This study also has some limitations. One limitation of this study lies in the use of a Tg+ mouse model that has intact CFTR channel . Although the Tg+ mice exhibit most of the hallmark features of human CF-like lung disease, the features of CF lung disease that are regulated by CFTR in immune cells remain intact in these mice. For instance, macrophage-specific CFTR-deficiency results in exaggerated lung inflammation in experimental model of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection . CFTR-deficient human macrophages display compromised phagocytosis, increased apoptosis, reduced ability to produce bactericidal reactive oxygen species, and altered transcriptional profiles – . CFTR deficiency in neutrophils compromises bactericidal potential and leads to neutrophilic inflammation in CF – . In light of these reports, we would have expected exaggerated bacterial clearance if the HMGB1-KO mice with the human CF-like lung disease, if such a model in CFTR-KO mice available. In summary, this study revealed several interesting findings. First, the deletion of HMGB1 in BALF myeloid cells resulted in increased neutrophil and eosinophil recruitment into the airspaces of Tg+ mice. Second, the deletion of HMGB1 in BALF myeloid cells resulted in morphological activation of macrophages in Tg+ mice. Third, the deletion of HMGB1 in myeloid cells induced significant increases in inflammatory mediators in the airspaces of Tg+ mice. Fourth, the deletion of HMGB1 in myeloid cells exaggerated airway mucus obstruction in Tg+ mice. Fifth, myeloid cell-specific deletion of HMGB1 exaggerated alveolar space enlargement feature of Tg+ mice. Finally, the myeloid cell-specific deletion of HMGB1 promoted bacteria clearance in the airspaces of Tg+ mice. Taken together, this study highlights previously unknown roles of HMGB1 in myeloid cell compartments in the context of pathological manifestations of muco-obstructive lung diseases. Introduction Sepsis, defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, is the leading cause of child mortality worldwide. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) bear a disproportionately high burden of sepsis, stemming from infections such as pneumonia, diarrhea, and malaria [ – ]. Mortality remains substantially greater for children in LMICs compared to high-income countries (HICs) for a multitude of reasons including: inadequate critical care capacity, shortages of trained healthcare workers (HCWs), higher levels of co-infections and malnutrition, as well as late identification of sepsis [ , ]. Sepsis encompasses a continuum of severity that ranges from sepsis to severe sepsis, septic shock, multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) and eventually death if untreated [ , , ]. Management of septic children is challenging even for experienced clinicians, as children often have dynamic and subtle physiologic changes which indicate worsening sepsis [ , ]. These challenges are compounded in settings with limited human and infrastructural resources for monitoring and diagnosis [ , ]. Frequent, accurate assessments of sepsis severity are important for effective patient management, allowing clinicians to intervene earlier, select the most appropriate treatments, and optimally utilize scarce healthcare resources to reduce morbidity and mortality [ ]. However, there remains a paucity of research from LMICs regarding the best methods for assessing sepsis severity for risk stratification and better directing care. While clinical scoring systems such as the pediatric logistic organ dysfunction (PELOD-2), pediatric sequential organ dysfunction assessment (pSOFA) scores, and the recent Phoenix Sepsis Score have been used largely in HICs, these scores are often not feasible to operationalize in LMICs due to their reliance on regular laboratory tests, clinical assessments from experienced HCWs, and relatively cumbersome calculations [ , – ]. Furthermore, while continuous telemetry monitoring is standard practice in HICs for sepsis care, in many LMICs, even intermittent vital sign checks to detect signs of progressive sepsis can place a substantial burden on HCWs with high patient-to-clinician ratios. Innovative digital technologies hold great potential to overcome some of the greatest barriers to improving sepsis care. Mobile health (mHealth) clinical decision support systems (CDSS), wearable devices, and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques have rapidly proliferated for a multitude of inpatient clinical applications, although few studies have been done in LMICs to date [ ]. The objectives of this study were to 1) determine the feasibility of using a wireless, wearable device for continuous remote vital sign monitoring in children with sepsis and 2) develop a clinical diagnostic model using primarily wearable device data to predict advanced sepsis (infection with organ dysfunction) among children in Bangladesh. The findings from this research will be used to develop this technology into a mHealth system which serves as a low-cost, remote telemetry monitor and CDSS, improving critical care capacity for pediatric sepsis in resource-limited settings ( ). Materials and methods Study design and setting This was a prospective, observational study of children with suspected sepsis who were admitted to the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b) Dhaka Hospital Intensive Care Unit (ICU). Dhaka Hospital provides free clinical services to >200,000 patients annually from a catchment area of more than 17 million people. Data were collected from February–December 2022. Due to an unprecedented outbreak of cholera, study activities were briefly paused in April 2022 as staff were diverted to assist with clinical care of patients. Ethical approval was obtained from the icddr,b Institutional Review Board comprising Research Review Committee and Ethical Review Committee and the Rhode Island Hospital Institutional Review Board. Study participants All patients between two months (prematurity-corrected) to 17 years of age admitted to the ICU with suspected sepsis were eligible for enrollment. Suspected sepsis was defined as meeting at least two systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria with suspected source of infection as determined by the treating physician, based on clinical practice during the enrollment period. Briefly, SIRS was defined according to Goldstein criteria as the presence of at least two of the following four criteria (one of which must be abnormal temperature or leukocyte count): 1) core temperature >38.5C or <36C; 2) tachycardia defined as mean heart rate (HR) >2 SD above normal for age or bradycardia <10 th percentile for age in children < 1 year; 3) mean respiratory rate (RR)>2 SD above normal for age or use of mechanical ventilation; 4) leukocyte count elevated or depressed for age [ ]. Trained study staff screened all pediatric patients consecutively for enrollment upon ICU admission 24 hours/day, 7 days/week. To ensure high-quality data collection and adherence to study protocols, a maximum of three simultaneous patients were enrolled. After screening, the parent/guardian of eligible patients was offered participation and informed consent (and assent for patients 11–17 years) was obtained in the local language, Bangla. Staff training A two-week pre-implementation phase and staff training period was conducted to ensure seamless integration of the wearable device monitoring system into clinical workflow prior to patient enrollment using a combination of didactics and hands-on training. Training focused on: 1) hands-on practice with the technology among all research staff (application, removal, replacement, and troubleshooting of the wearable device, smartphone operation, data quality monitoring, etc.) 2) logistics of implementing the technology including ensuring electrical and internet connectivity 3) collection of all clinical and laboratory data and assessments of sepsis severity. Dedicated research nurses and physicians were hired and trained to screen and enroll patients, obtain informed consent, collect data, and monitor data quality. Study procedures and data collection After patient enrollment, study staff collected demographic and clinical data on all patients, including age, sex, height, weight, and mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC). Staff then applied a VitalPatch (VitalConnect, Inc., San Jose, CA), a medical grade wearable biosensor device, to the patient’s torso. The lightweight (13g), water-resistant, flexible device was applied via the device’s adhesive after cleaning the skin with an alcohol pad. An anterior chest wall position was used for most patients; for very small children (roughly <4kg) a posterior chest wall position was used as it was found this improved adhesion to the chest ( ). The device continuously transmitted the following data: single-lead ECG signal, three-dimensional accelerometer, uncalibrated skin temperature via Bluetooth to a connected Android (Samsung Galaxy A10e) smartphone ( ) which then transmitted data continuously to the remote Cloud servers run by PhysIQ, Inc. Real-time ECG and vital sign data were accessible to remote study investigators via a web browser-based monitoring dashboard ( ). Raw biosignal waveform data from the device was extracted and analyzed to generate the following parameters at one-minute intervals for the duration of the patient’s enrollment: HR, RR, heart rate variability (HRV), and skin and core temperature (T). Devices were removed at patient discharge by slowly peeling off the device from the skin. Laboratory testing including complete blood count, electrolytes, glucose, renal function, hepatic function panel, lactate, blood gas, and coagulation panel were obtained upon admission, then twice daily (every 12 hours approximately). For patients with prolonged ICU admissions (four or more days), laboratory testing was reduced to once daily as deemed appropriate and according to clinical necessity by the treating physicians. Clinical exams and vital sign assessments were documented by study staff every hour including Glasgow Coma Score (GCS), manual vital signs (BP, HR, RR, T, SpO2), capillary refill time, and urine output, for determination of sepsis state using the Goldstein criteria and pSOFA score [ , ]. Patients enrolled in the study received routine care for sepsis according to institutional protocols which included clinical examinations, radiographs and ultrasound, administration of IV fluids, antibiotics, vasopressors, blood products, and use of bubble continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and mechanical ventilation as per standard guidelines followed in the ICU [ – ]. All data obtained during routine clinical care were entered on case report forms (CRF) separate from usual icddr,b clinical documentation. Outcomes The primary outcome of interest was the development of advanced sepsis defined as pSOFA score > 8 (indicative of organ dysfunction and/or septic shock) calculated twice daily (approximately every 12 hours) by a research physician after the conclusion of the study. Researchers were thus blinded to the primary outcome during the conduct of the study. This outcome was chosen given its indication of clinically actionable sepsis states which often warrant higher level of care or more intensive treatments (e.g., vasopressors in shock). Additionally, calculation of pSOFA scores twice daily increased the number of outcomes available given the relatively small cohort. As a secondary outcome, we compared the time to recognition of advanced sepsis as determined using the clinical model compared to standard clinical documentation. In addition, we evaluated the feasibility, quality, correlation, and agreement of data collected from the wearable device, as described below.
